As of 230 AM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Increasing clouds with a few light showers or 
sprinkles possible through this evening. Unseasonably warm 
conditions continue through Thursday.

High pressure continues to shift farther offshore this 
afternoon as a cold front slowly approaches from the west. Cloud
cover has increased more quickly than anticipated over much of 
the area. In addition, a few sprinkles and light rain showers 
have developed, especially across the southern half of the area,
as moisture increases ahead of the next system. Expect this 
activity to remain generally light and spotty through this 
evening, with many locations staying dry. The increased cloud 
cover will likely limit additional warming this afternoon, 
although temperatures remain well above normal for early 
November.

Mostly cloudy skies are expected tonight as additional mid- 
level moisture streams into the region. Rain chances gradually 
increase across our western zones tonight, with the highest PoPs
across far western Louisa, Fluvanna, and Prince Edward 
counties. Temperatures remain mild with lows generally in the 
upper 50s to lower 60s. 

Another warm day is anticipated for Thursday as southerly flow 
increases ahead of the approaching front. High temperatures 
likely climb into the mid to upper 70s with a few locations 
across SE VA and NE NC approaching 80 degrees. Skies will remain
mostly cloudy, and a few isolated showers or sprinkles will be 
possible during the day. However, the more widespread rainfall 
is expected to hold off until Thursday night. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Widespread moderate to locally heavy rainfall 
is expected Thursday night through Friday, with a few 
thunderstorms possible.

Confidence continues to increase in a widespread rainfall event
Thursday night through Friday as a slow-moving cold front 
approaches and crosses the region. Rain should develop across 
western portions of the area late Thursday night before becoming
more widespread Friday morning. The primary forecast challenge 
continues to be the placement and magnitude of the heaviest 
rainfall, particularly given the potential for a wave of low 
pressure to develop and track northeast along the frontal 
boundary Friday. 

The latest 12z guidance has trended wetter, with the ECMWF 
shifting the axis of heavier precipitation a bit farther to the 
northwest compared to its previous runs. The 12z EPS has 
followed this trend, with increasing probabilities of exceeding 
both 1 and 2 inches across eastern portions of the area. The EPS
mean now depicts rainfall amounts of 1.5 to locally over 2 
inches across portions of SE VA and the MD Eastern Shore, with 
considerably lower amounts farther inland. Meanwhile, the 12z 
GFS remains notably wetter and farther northwest, depicting 
localized amounts of 3 to 4 inches from central VA northeastward
toward the Eastern Shore. 

There is a favorable environment for locally heavy rainfall, 
with PWATs forecast to increase to 200+ percent of normal for 
early November. In addition, guidance suggests a corridor of 
enhanced mid-level frontogenesis and strong ascent associated 
with the frontal boundary and a potential developing wave of low
pressure. This could support a southwest to northeast oriented 
band of moderate to locally heavy rainfall, potentially 
persisting over some locations for several hours. While 
confidence in widespread rainfall has increased, uncertainty 
still remains regarding the precise location and intensity of 
this band. In general, rainfall amounts of 0.50 to 1.50” appears
reasonable for much of the area with 1.5 to 2” inches or more 
possible across portions of eastern VA and the MD Eastern Shore.

A few embedded thunderstorms will also be possible Friday, 
particularly across SE VA and NE NC. Forecast soundings indicate
increasing deep-layer shear, generally 30 to 40 kts, with 
modest surface based instability developing in the warm sector 
(~500 J/kg MLCAPE). While the environment could support a few 
stronger storms, widespread cloud cover and ongoing 
precipitation will likely substantially limit destabilization. 
As a result, organized severe weather is generally not 
anticipated, though an isolated damaging wind gust cannot be 
completely ruled out across far SE portions of the area. 

Rainfall gradually diminishes from west to east later Friday 
afternoon into Friday night as the cold front pushes offshore. 
Drier and cooler conditions return for the weekend as northwest 
flow develops behind the front. High temperatures generally 
return to the 60s Saturday and Sunday with seasonably cool 
overnight lows.
